items.title: The sun, Earth, Jupiter and white dwarfs: Potential traps for dark matter
items.snippet: Dark matter continues to evade direct detection. Its slower-moving particles might leave signals too faint for detectors to register, yet be more easily captured by planets and stars. As they accumulate inside these bodies, they could produce effects that existing instruments would allow us to search for.

items.title: Flat optics roadmap charts path toward smaller imaging and sensing systems
items.snippet: For centuries, optical systems have relied on lenses, mirrors and other components that manipulate light through their shape and size. Today, advances in nanotechnology are enabling a different approach. Researchers can now engineer materials at scales smaller than the wavelength of light, creating ultrathin optical components that offer new ways to control how light behaves.

items.title: Early black holes may have grown through productive chaos
items.snippet: When the universe was less than 700 million years old, the supermassive black hole powering a quasar called J0313-1806 had already grown to about 3 billion times the mass of the sun. It is one of the most extreme examples of a puzzle that has occupied astrophysicists for two decades: How did supermassive black holes grow so big so quickly?
